tier_reason: eBACS/SUPERCOP is a well-known independent suite. On the hertz page (Ryzen 7 7700) aegis128l runs at 0.18-0.19 cycles/byte and aes256gcmv1 at 0.55-0.57. The public harness and web-impl pages give compiler, flags and CPU, but the measured aegis128l code (the uncredited 'aesnib' implementation) is not shown to be libaegis. The fastest AES-GCM is also Dolbeau's VAES code, not OpenSSL, so this is B, not A.

corrections.workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP AEAD 'long+0 encrypt' benchmark: cycles/byte for long messages with no associated data, computed as 1/1920 of the cycle-count difference between a 2048-byte and a 128-byte message (not 1536-byte messages)
corrections.claimed_speedup: long+0 encrypt quartiles on hertz: aegis128l 0.18/0.19/0.19 cycles/byte vs aes256gcmv1 0.55/0.56/0.57 cycles/byte, about 2.9-3x faster (derived from page data). 1536+1536 encrypt: aegis128l 0.20-0.21 vs aes256gcmv1 0.55-0.56. The wider AEGIS-128X4 variant (also in libaegis) measures 0.07-0.08 cycles/byte long+0, about 7-8x (derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: AES-256-GCM (SUPERCOP aes256gcmv1; on this host the fastest implementation is Romain Dolbeau's VAES code; the OpenSSL wrapper 'opensslnew' is also measured and is slower)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From the eBACS web-impl pages (SUPERCOP 20260831, hertz). Fastest aegis128l implementation 'aesnib': clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall. Fastest aes256gcmv1 implementation 'dolbeau/vaesenc-int': clang -march=native -Os -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 146 stars; AEGIS is now published as RFC 10032 (linked from the libaegis README) and is also shipped inside libsodium
corrections.caveats: eBACS measures SUPERCOP's own AEGIS implementations, not libaegis. The winning aegis128l code on hertz is 'aesnib' (no author credited); Frank Denis's sodium-aesni (libsodium) scores close behind, and the aegis128x2/x4 code in SUPERCOP is credited to Frank Denis. The aes256gcmv1 row is the best of several AES-GCM implementations. On hertz that is dolbeau/vaesenc-int. The OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew) is slower in the web-impl selection-time column: about 5764 for opensslnew vs 3258 for dolbeau and 1241 for aegis128l aesnib, so the gap against OpenSSL itself is likely larger than 3x. Compiler and flags ARE disclosed on the per-machine web-impl pages. libaegis's own README chart (img/bench-encryption.png, first-party, 16 KB encryption) does state its CPUs. On AMD Zen 4 with turbo off: aegis128l 208.44 Gb/s vs aes256-gcm (BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s. On Apple M1: 114.61 vs 41.6 Gb/s. The chart's baseline is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL, and the libaegis benchmark.zig does not include AES-GCM.

notes: The numbers are accurate and belong to the aegis128l and aes256gcmv1 rows. The workload wrongly said 1536-byte messages; 'long' is the 2048-vs-128-byte differential. The record's caveats wrongly said compiler flags were undisclosed and the README charts had no CPU, and both are corrected. Tier would be A for the AEGIS algorithm vs OpenSSL AES-GCM, but the measured code is not shown to be libaegis's.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. Netgate's AsiaBSDCon 2023 paper (linked from the project wiki's Links page) gives head-to-head numbers: IPsec-MB 18.1 Gbps vs OpenSSL 10.4 Gbps for AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256, plus VPN throughput vs FreeBSD's default OCF kernel crypto. The OpenSSL comparison names no CPU model, uses mismatched block sizes, and gives no compiler/flags or benchmark code, and it is not a well-known benchmark suite, so this is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Netgate AsiaBSDCon 2023 paper: on an AVX2 test host, IPsec-MB did 18.1 Gbps AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 on 1400-byte blocks vs OpenSSL's maximum of 10.4 Gbps on 16 kB blocks, about 1.7x (derived from page data). In pfSense/FreeBSD VPN tests, the IIMB engine was compared with FreeBSD's default OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) on Ryzen 5 5600 VMs: OpenVPN DCO AES-256-GCM async 10 vs 6.0 Gbps; ChaCha20-Poly1305 async 7.0 vs 4.10 Gbps; IPsec-ESP AES-128-GCM async 7.68 vs 4.46 Gbps. On the Netgate SG-8200 (Atom C3758), OpenVPN AES-256-GCM async was 2.50 vs 1.50 Gbps.
corrections.baseline: OpenSSL (AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput) and FreeBSD OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) default kernel crypto (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 VPN throughput)
corrections.workload: Raw AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput vs OpenSSL on an AVX2 host, plus end-to-end iperf3 VPN throughput (OpenVPN DCO, IPsec-ESP, WireGuard) in pfSense/FreeBSD with an IIMB-based engine replacing OCF as the in-kernel crypto provider
corrections.hardware: OpenSSL comparison: unnamed 'test host with AVX2'. VPN tests: AMD Ryzen 5 5600 (KVM/QEMU VMs running FreeBSD-CURRENT) and Netgate SG-8200 (Intel Atom C3758).
corrections.caveats: The only OpenSSL head-to-head is one sentence in a downstream user's (Netgate) paper. It covers AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256, not AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, uses mismatched block sizes (1400 B for IPsec-MB vs 16 kB for OpenSSL), and names no CPU model or compiler. The AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 gains are measured against FreeBSD's OCF framework, not OpenSSL, in end-to-end VPN throughput, so part of the gain comes from the new engine's job batching and async handling, not only the library's kernels. The paper's ARM (SG-1100) results use ISA-L AES and OpenSSL ChaCha20-Poly1305, not intel-ipsec-mb. Intel's own white paper (2012) and the DPDK 25.11 Intel crypto performance report give absolute throughput only, with no OpenSSL comparison. The vendored ML-DSA/ML-KEM code is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.OpenSSL); the rest is BSD-3-Clause, and both are OSI-approved.

notes: I found a real numbers page via the project wiki's Links page, so I upgraded D to C (verdict confirm). If the orchestrator counts AsiaBSDCon as peer-reviewed it could argue B, but the OpenSSL comparison itself has almost no methodology. I changed usability from 'mixed' to 'copyable' because all code is under OSI licenses (BSD-3-Clause plus Apache-2.0 vendored parts). numbers_found_on_page refers to the corrected claimed_speedup; the original record claimed no numbers.
